title: Lists, tuples, dictionaries & sets
summary: Meet Python's four core collections — store many values, look them up by key, and choose the right structure for each job.
objectives: Create and index lists, and change them in place
Use tuples for fixed, unchangeable groups of values
Store and retrieve data by key with dictionaries
Use sets to hold unique values and do membership tests fast
Choose the right collection for a given problem

quiz.q: Which collection is ordered and changeable (mutable)?
quiz.why: A list is ordered and mutable — you can change, add, and remove items after creating it.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a list and a tuple?
quiz.answer: A list is mutable (can be changed); a tuple is immutable (fixed once created).
quiz.why: Use a tuple when the group of values should never change, such as a coordinate (x, y).

quiz.q: How do you get the value for the key "name" from a dictionary called user?
quiz.why: Dictionaries are accessed with square brackets and the key: user["name"].

quiz.q: What happens when you add a duplicate value to a set?
options: It is ignored — sets keep only unique values
quiz.why: Sets store only unique values, so adding a duplicate simply has no effect.

quiz.answer: The number of items in the list.
quiz.why: len() works on any collection and gives you its size — handy for loops and checks.

quiz.q: Which collection should you use to count unique visitors to a website?
quiz.answer: A set — it automatically removes duplicates so only distinct visitors remain.
quiz.why: Sets discard repeats, so the size of the set equals the number of unique values.

resources.label: Real Python — Lists and Tuples in Python

body_markdown:
## Why collections?

So far you have stored one value per variable. Real data comes in groups: a list of marks, a row of coordinates, a record of a person, a set of tags. Python gives you four core **collections** to hold groups of values, and choosing the right one makes your code clearer and faster.

The four are: **list**, **tuple**, **dictionary**, and **set**.

## Lists — ordered and changeable

A **list** keeps items in order and lets you change them. Write it with square brackets. You reach an item by its **index**, counting from zero.

```python
scores = [70, 85, 90]
print(scores[0])      # 70 (first item)
scores.append(60)     # add to the end
scores[1] = 88        # change an item
print(len(scores))    # 4
```

## Tuples — fixed and unchangeable

A **tuple** looks like a list but uses round brackets and cannot be changed after it is made — it is **immutable**. Use it for groups that should stay fixed, like an (x, y) point.

```python
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point          # unpack into two variables
print(x, y)           # 3 4
# point[0] = 9        # would raise an error
```

## Dictionaries — look up by key

A **dictionary** stores **key-value** pairs. Instead of a numeric index, you look things up by a meaningful key. Write it with curly braces and colons.

```python
user = {"name": "Dami", "age": 25}
print(user["name"])       # Dami
user["age"] = 26          # update a value
user["city"] = "Lagos"    # add a new pair
for key, value in user.items():
    print(key, "->", value)
```

## Sets — unique values only

A **set** holds only **unique** values and has no order. It is perfect for removing duplicates and for fast membership tests.

```python
tags = {"python", "git", "python"}
print(tags)               # {'python', 'git'} — duplicate gone
tags.add("sql")
print("git" in tags)      # True
```

## Choosing the right one

Use a **list** for an ordered, changeable sequence. Use a **tuple** for a fixed group. Use a **dictionary** to label data with keys. Use a **set** for uniqueness and fast lookups.

## Your task

Build a small contacts program: keep each contact as a **dictionary**, store all contacts in a **list**, and use a **set** to track which cities appear.

slides.title: Lists, tuples, dictionaries & sets
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month One of your journey from maths graduate to A I engineer. In this lesson we meet Python's four core collections: lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets. These are the workhorses you'll use to store and organise data in almost every program you ever write. By the end you'll know what each one does and, just as importantly, when to reach for each one.

slides.title: Why collections?
bullets: Four core tools: list, tuple, dict, set.
slides.narration: So far each variable has held a single value. But real data almost always comes in groups: a list of exam marks, a record describing a person, a set of unique tags. Python gives us four core collections to hold these groups. Picking the right one for the job makes your code easier to read and often much faster.

slides.title: Lists: ordered & changeable
bullets: Reach items by index, counting from zero.
slides.code:
scores = [70, 85, 90]
print(scores[0])    # 70
scores.append(60)   # add
scores[1] = 88      # change
slides.narration: First, the list. A list keeps items in order and lets you change them. We write it with square brackets. To reach an item we use its index, and Python counts from zero, so scores at index zero is the first item, seventy. We can append to add to the end, and assign to change an item. Lists are your everyday go-to collection.

slides.title: Looping over a list
bullets: for loops visit each item in turn.
len() gives the number of items.
slides.code:
scores = [70, 85, 90]
for s in scores:
    print(s)
print(len(scores))   # 3
slides.narration: Because a list is ordered, looping over it is simple and natural. A for loop visits each item in turn, so this prints seventy, eighty-five, and ninety on their own lines. The len function tells us how many items are in the list. You'll use this pattern constantly, so get comfortable with it now.

slides.title: Tuples: fixed & unchangeable
bullets: Great for fixed groups like (x, y).
slides.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)   # 3 4
slides.narration: A tuple looks like a list but uses round brackets, and here's the key difference: once you make a tuple, you cannot change it. We say it's immutable. That sounds like a limitation, but it's perfect for groups that should stay fixed, like a coordinate point. A neat trick is unpacking: we pull the two values straight out into x and y in one line.

slides.title: Dictionaries: look up by key
bullets: Look up by a meaningful key, not a number.
slides.narration: Now the dictionary, one of the most useful tools in Python. Instead of a numeric index, a dictionary stores key-value pairs, so you look things up by a meaningful key. Here user square-bracket name gives us Dami. We can update existing values or add brand-new pairs at any time. Think of it as a labelled drawer for your data.

slides.title: Looping over a dictionary
bullets: Read like a record or a small table.
slides.narration: To loop through a dictionary we usually use the items method, which hands us each key and its value together. This prints name arrow Dami, then age arrow twenty-five. Modern Python keeps dictionaries in the order you added things, so what you put in is the order you get back out. This makes dictionaries great for representing records.

slides.title: Sets: unique values only
bullets: Curly braces, but values not pairs.
slides.narration: Last is the set. A set holds only unique values and has no order. Watch what happens here: we add python twice, but the set keeps just one copy. That makes sets brilliant for removing duplicates. They're also extremely fast at answering the question is this value in here, using the in keyword. If you ever need to count unique things, a set is your friend.

slides.title: Choosing the right one
bullets: Tuple: fixed group that won't change.
slides.narration: So how do you choose? Reach for a list when you have an ordered sequence you'll change. Reach for a tuple when the group should stay fixed. Reach for a dictionary when you want to label data with meaningful keys. And reach for a set when you care about uniqueness or need fast membership checks. With practice this choice becomes second nature.
